## Introduction

Since more than two decades, the **stats** package serves as a home for
well-established statistical analysis tools, including linear and
generalized linear models or a versatile collection of statistical
test procedures featuring `*.test()` user interfaces. In some cases, 
such as `t.test()`, `var.test()`, or `binom.test()`, the null and alternative
hypotheses are formulated in terms of a parametric model. Model diagnostics
and power analysis is relatively simple in this situation and corresponding
functionality is provided by **stats**, for example as `qqnorm()`,
`power.t.test()` etc.

Other procedures are fully nonparametric. The Smirnov two-sample test, for
example, allows testing the null of equal distributions against arbitrary
alternatives in the two-sample oneway layout via `ks.test()`.

For yet another group of test procedures it is harder to understand the
underlying model. This makes model diagnostics and also power analysis much
more challenging, which explains the absence of, for example,
`power.wilcox.test()` or `power.friedman.test()` from the **stats** package.

Beginning with R version 4.6.0, the novel `free1way()` function provides a
unified interface to semiparametrically efficient population and permutation
inference in distribution-free stratified K-sample oneway layouts. This post
explains the rationale of this model class and discusses how existing test
procedures, for example `kruskal.test()`, are enhanced by this new tool.

## Distribution-free oneway layouts

When comparing the distributions of some outcome in certain experimental
groups, we might refrain from making assumptions regarding the distribution
function in one of these groups (typically a control group corresponding to
the first factor level, say $F_0$) while, at the same time, assuming that the
distribution functions in the remaining groups are simple transformations of
this control distribution characterized by a single parameter. 
Under this model, we assume that the distribution function in the second group
$F_1$ is 
a function of distribution function in the control group $F_0$ and a
parameter $\tau$. For example 
$F_1 = F_0^{\exp(-\tau)}$, with $\tau$ being our unknown treatment effect
parameter to be estimated.

This idea, going back to Erich Lehmann's 1953 paper on 
[The Power of Rank Tests](https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177729080), allows
the formulation of many statistical tests for the composite null $\tau = 0$ or
one-sided alternatives. As an
example, consider the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney rank sum test. It turns out that
this classical test is the score test under the proportional-odds model
$$
\frac{F_1}{1 - F_1} = \exp(-\tau) \frac{F_0}{1 - F_0}
$$
whose parameters $F_0$ and $\tau$ can be estimated by maximising the
empirical log-likelihood. If more than two samples are to be compared, the
model corresponds to the Kruskal-Wallis test.

As an illustration, consider the example presented in the manual page of
`kruskal.test()`:

```{r, fig.show = "hide"}
## Hollander & Wolfe (1973), 116.
## Mucociliary efficiency from the rate of removal of dust in normal
##  subjects, subjects with obstructive airway disease, and subjects
##  with asbestosis.
example(kruskal.test, echo = FALSE)
levels(g) <- c("Normal", "COPD", "Asbestosis")
(kt <- kruskal.test(x ~ g))
(ft <- free1way(x ~ g))
```

The test statistics and p-values are identical, but the print method of the
latter procedure informs about the alternative this test is powerful (in
fact, the locally most powerful test) against.

In contrast to the classical implementation in `kruskal.test()` (where
`coef(kt)` comes back empty handed), the novel
`free1way()` is aware of the semiparametric nature of the model and allows
to access the estimated log-odds ratios along with a confidence interval (a
Rao score interval is presented here):

```{r}
cbind(LogOR = coef(ft),
      confint(ft, test = "Rao"))
```

The data analysis could also question the sample size needed to demonstrate
an overall effect when the true log-odds ratios are close to the one
estimated from this dataset

```{r}
power.free1way.test(delta = coef(ft), power = .8)
```

## Features

Binary, ordered categorical, numeric and possibly right-censored outcomes
can be analyzed using `free1way()`. In stratified designs, strata can be
specified as blocks. Wald, likelihood-ratio and Rao score tests and
confidence intervals are available. In addition, permutation tests
(asymptotic and resampling-based, exact for two-sample proportional odds
models) can be performed to test hypotheses. Multiple comparisons can be
conducted via an interface to the
[multcomp package](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.multcomp). Similar to
Firth's method in binary GLMs, penalisation via Jeffreys' prior is implemented.

## Resources

In addition to the documentation, examples, and tests provided in the
**stats** package, a dedicated [free1way.docreg package](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.free1way.docreg)
features two vignettes explaining the implementation and
statistical framework in depths, along additional regression tests comparing
the implementation against benchmarks such as `rms::orm()` 
([rms package](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.rms)),
`MASS::polr()` 
([MASS package](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.MASS)), or
`tram::Polr()` 
([tram package](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.tram)).
